messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Tomás

Tomás was twenty-one when his brother was stabbed outside a bar in South Boston. The attack happened on a Friday night in October; Tomás was not there, but he arrived at the hospital while the emergency team was still working. What he remembers most vividly is not the doctors' words or the machines, but the smell—antiseptic mixed with something metallic and warm, a scent that seemed to lodge itself permanently in his nostrils. His brother survived, but the injury left him partially paralyzed on his left side. Tomás watched the man who had been his closest friend transform into someone trapped in a body that no longer obeyed him. The attacker was never caught.

In the weeks that followed, Tomás found himself hypervigilant in ways he could not control. When his wife, Elena, moved too quickly to hand him something, his entire body would tense; he would flinch, his heart racing, his hands suddenly clammy. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and he could not seem to override the response even when he knew rationally that Elena was simply reaching for the remote or that a friend was standing to leave. The threat felt immediate and undeniable, as if his body had learned something his mind could not unlearn. When he tried to explain this to Elena, he found himself unable to put the experience into words—the memory existed as vivid, fragmented images rather than narrative. He could see his brother's face in the ambulance, the specific angle of the paramedic's hands, the exact pattern of the hospital tiles, but when he tried to speak about it, the words dissolved.

These intrusive visual memories became so overwhelming that Tomás began to avoid anything that might trigger them. He stopped watching television entirely, terrified that a crime drama or news report might suddenly thrust him back into that hospital corridor. He refused to read articles about violence, even when Elena tried to discuss current events. But the memories did not stay contained to screens. Whenever he noticed someone acting suspiciously—a stranger crossing the street with their hands in their pockets, a neighbor he did not recognize lingering near their building—the photographic clarity of the attack flooded back. He would feel as though it were happening again, his body responding as if the danger were present and immediate. When Elena mentioned her family's upcoming reunion, the casual remark about seeing relatives triggered a cascade of panic; he could not explain why comments about family felt dangerous, only that they seemed to pull at something deep and uncontrollable within him.

To manage the overwhelming sensations, Tomás began avoiding being alone. He could not sit by himself in a room without the anxiety building to an intolerable pitch, so he followed Elena from room to room, clinging to her presence as though it were a lifeline. But isolation found him anyway. He had stopped working at the construction company where he had labored since high school—the unpredictability of the job site, the sudden noises, the presence of strangers, all felt impossible to navigate. His identity as a reliable worker, as someone who built things and took pride in his strength, evaporated. He was no longer capable of the things that had defined him. His body, which had always been competent and strong, had become an enemy—reacting with terror when there was no threat, refusing to sleep, keeping him locked in a state of exhaustion that made everything worse.

The nights became particularly unbearable. Sleep would not come, or when it did, he would wake gasping, the smell of the hospital flooding his nostrils even though he was safe in his bed. When the insomnia and the intrusive images became too much, when the feeling of being trapped in his own malfunctioning body became unbearable, Tomás began to hurt himself—pressing his fingernails into his palms, holding ice against his skin until it burned—seeking physical pain as a way to discharge the overwhelming emotional intensity. The pain was clarifying in a way nothing else was. But these acts of self-harm only deepened his conviction that he could not rely on himself, that something fundamental had broken. Elena found him one night and wept, and Tomás realized he had become a source of fear rather than comfort in his own marriage. He is now seeking help, terrified that the fragmentation and hypervigilance will never resolve, but also harboring a desperate hope that someone might help him understand why his own body has become his enemy and whether he might ever feel safe again.
